hero.title: Children’s dentistry
hero.lead: A good experience early on shapes how children feel about the dentist for life. We keep visits calm, friendly and unhurried.

intro.heading: Why baby teeth matter
intro.html:
Baby teeth help children chew, speak clearly and hold space for adult teeth. Decay in baby teeth can cause pain and infection, and can affect the adult teeth developing underneath.

Regular visits let your dentist check how teeth and jaws are developing, apply preventive care where it helps, and give you practical advice for brushing and diet at each age.

explain.heading: Helping your child feel ready
explain.intro: A few simple things that make the first visit easier.

items.title: Keep it low-key
items.text: Talk about the visit in a matter-of-fact way. Words like “hurt” or “needle” can plant worries that weren’t there.

items.title: Pick a good time
items.text: Morning appointments often suit younger children, when they’re rested and fed.

items.title: Come along together
items.text: Children can watch a parent or sibling have a check-up first, so they know what to expect.

items.title: Tell us about worries
items.text: Let reception know if your child is nervous or has had a tough experience before.

care.heading: Caring for your child’s teeth at home
items: Brush twice a day with a soft, small-headed brush. Supervise brushing until your child can do it well, usually around 7 or 8.
Water only from the first tooth to 18 months unless advised otherwise; low-fluoride children’s toothpaste from 18 months to 6 years; standard fluoride toothpaste from 6 years. Use a pea-sized amount.
Water is the best drink. Avoid putting children to bed with a bottle of milk or juice, and keep sweet snacks to mealtimes.
If your child plays contact sport, ask about a custom mouthguard.

faqs: When should my child first visit?
Australian guidance suggests when the first teeth come through, or by around 12 months of age.
What is the Child Dental Benefits Schedule?

An Australian Government program that helps eligible families with the cost of some basic dental services for children. Eligibility depends on age and on certain government payments, and benefits are capped. Check with Services Australia.
My child is scared. What should I do?
Let us know when you book. Keep your own language calm and matter-of-fact, and let your child watch someone else in the family have a check-up first if that helps.
